content: Lichen planus is an inflammatory condition that primarily affects the skin and oral mucosa. It is also known by other terms such as ruber planus and is characterized by the presence of Wickham's striae, which are fine, white, lacy streaks often seen on the mucosal surfaces. Historical Perspective and Classification A specific variant of lichen planus, known as lichen planopilaris, occurs on the scalp and can lead to permanent scarring alopecia if left untreated. This scarring results in irreversible hair loss. The Cicatricial Alopecia Research Foundation is a non-profit organization that provides resources and support for individuals affected by lichen planopilaris. Pathophysiology and Causes The exact cause of lichen planus remains unknown. However, lichen planus-like rashes, referred to as lichenoid reactions, can occur as allergic responses to certain medications, including those used to treat high blood pressure, heart disease, and arthritis. These reactions are termed lichenoid mucositis when they affect the mucosa and lichenoid dermatitis when they involve the skin. Lichen planus has also been associated with chronic hepatitis C virus infection and may serve as a cutaneous manifestation of chronic graft-versus-host disease. Stress has been suggested as a potential trigger for true lichen planus, with lesions appearing on the skin or mucosa during periods of heightened stress in affected individuals. Common Causes Medications such as bendrofluazide, chloroquine, gold salts, hydrochlorothiazide, mepacrine, methyldopa, and penicillamine have been implicated in lichenoid reactions. Other associated conditions include hepatitis C, graft-versus-host disease, and stress. Differential Diagnosis The clinical presentation of lichen planus can mimic other conditions, including: Lichenoid drug reactions Discoid lupus erythematosus Chronic ulcerative stomatitis Pemphigus vulgaris Benign mucous membrane pemphigoid Oral leukoplakia Frictional keratosis A biopsy is often necessary to identify histological features that differentiate lichen planus from these conditions. Epidemiology and Demographics Lichen planus is rare in children and most commonly affects middle-aged adults. Women are more frequently affected than men, with a female-to-male ratio of 3:2. Risk Factors Risk factors for lichen planus include exposure to certain medications, dyes, and chemicals (e.g., gold, antibiotics, arsenic, iodides, chloroquine, quinacrine, quinidine, phenothiazines, and diuretics) and underlying disorders such as hepatitis C. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis Lichen planus is generally not harmful and often resolves with treatment, typically clearing within 18 months. However, it may persist for weeks to months and can recur intermittently over years. If caused by a medication, the rash usually resolves once the offending drug is discontinued. A notable complication is the potential for long-standing oral ulcers to develop into oral cancer. Diagnosis Symptoms The microscopic appearance of lichen planus is pathognomonic and includes: Hyperparakeratosis with thickening of the granular cell layer A saw-tooth appearance of the rete pegs Degeneration of the basal cell layer Infiltration of inflammatory cells into the subepithelial connective tissue Other symptoms may include: Scarring alopecia Genital ulcers Gum pathology Hyperkeratosis Koebner phenomenon Lichenoid dermatitis Mucosal leukoplakia Nail pitting Oral ulceration Pruritus Tongue abnormalities Physical Examination The classic rash of lichen planus is described by the 5 P's: pruritic, planar, purple, polygonal papules. Commonly affected areas include the wrists and ankles. The rash often heals with persistent blue-black or brownish discoloration. Morphological variations of the rash may occur, and cutaneous lesions may wax and wane over time. Oral lesions tend to persist longer than cutaneous ones. Oral Manifestations Oral lichen planus may present in three forms: 1. Reticular form: The most common presentation, characterized by white lacy streaks (Wickham's striae) or small papules on the mucosa. These lesions are typically bilateral and asymptomatic. 2. Bullous form: Fluid-filled vesicles that project from the surface. 3. Erosive form: Erythematous, ulcerated areas that are often painful. These lesions may occur in multiple areas of the mouth or be localized, such as on the gums, resembling desquamative gingivitis. Wickham's striae may be seen near these ulcerated areas. This form carries a risk of malignant transformation. Esophageal Involvement Rarely, lichen planus may involve the esophagus, presenting as erosive esophagitis and stricturing. It has been hypothesized as a precursor to esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Genital Involvement Lichen planus can also affect the genital mucosa, presenting as vulvovaginal-gingival lichen planus. It may resemble other dermatological conditions such as atopic dermatitis and psoriasis. Skin-only lichen planus is generally easier to treat compared to cases involving oral and genital lesions. Treatment Currently, there is no definitive cure for lichen planus. However, various medications, including oral and topical steroids, are used to reduce inflammation and manage symptoms. The condition may enter a dormant state following treatment, but flare-ups can occur years after it is considered resolved.
